title: Cultural fire management
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:50Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank point 'Care for Country' is broader, covering the whole concept of Country and custodianship, and only mentions cultural burning in passing, while the new point is specifically about the purpose and benefits of cool, patchy cultural burns.

draft.title: Cultural fire management
card: First Nations Australians have used fire to care for Country for many thousands of years. The burns are planned using cultural knowledge passed down over generations.
The burns are cool and small, and they burn in patches. They clear grass, leaf litter and twigs on the ground, which are fuel, but they leave a mosaic of burnt and unburnt ground.
Timing matters. Burns are done at the right time of year, often in the cooler months, when fires burn slowly and can be controlled.
Less fuel lowers the risk of large, hot bushfires. Unburnt patches give animals shelter, and fire helps some plants to regrow or set seed.
draft.remember: Small, cool, patchy burns at the right time cut fuel and protect Country.

a.q: Why are cultural burns done as cool, small and patchy fires?
opts: They clear ground fuel but leave unburnt areas for wildlife
They burn every tree so that new forest can grow
They stop all fire from ever reaching the area again
They clear the whole area quickly so that it is bare
a.why: Cool, patchy burns remove fuel on the ground while leaving unburnt patches where animals shelter. A hot fire that clears everything is the opposite of the aim, which is to lower the risk of large bushfires, not to remove all plants.
a.clue: Think about what is cleared and what is left behind.

b.q: A ranger group in the Northern Territory lights small burns on the ground in the cooler months. How does this help reduce the risk of a large bushfire later in the year?
opts: It removes fuel, so later fires burn with less heat
It makes the ground wetter, so later fires cannot start
It removes all plants, so there is nothing left to burn
It scares off animals, so fewer fires are lit by accident
b.why: Burning in the cooler months removes grass and litter, which are fuel. With less fuel, a later fire is smaller and less intense. It does not make the ground wetter, and it does not remove all plants because the burns are patchy.
b.clue: Think about what fire needs to keep burning.

a.best: They clear ground fuel but leave unburnt areas for wildlife

b.best: It removes fuel, so later fires burn with less heat

problems.detail: All three wrong options use extreme words ('the whole area', 'all fire from ever', 'every tree'). The right option is the only measured one, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The facts and both answers are sound. In question a, all three wrong options are extreme ('whole', 'all ... ever', 'every'), which makes the right answer easy to spot.

a.q: Why are cultural burns done as cool, small and patchy fires?
opts: They clear ground fuel but leave unburnt areas for wildlife
They burn the tree canopy but leave ground litter in place
They clear ground cover so animals move away to safer areas
They let the fire spread further so more land gets cleared
a.why: Cool, patchy burns remove grass, leaf litter and twigs on the ground while leaving unburnt patches where animals can shelter. They do not aim to push animals away or clear more land: the burns are kept small, and the unburnt patches are there to protect wildlife.
a.clue: Think about what is cleared and what is left behind.
